records.toxicity_detail: NC State's Poison block for this species is human-scoped: it sits under the heading "Poisonous to Humans:" and the page's own callout reads "This plant has low severity poison characteristics.", with Poison Severity rendered as "Low". Poison Symptoms: "CAUSES ONLY LOW TOXICITY IF EATEN. SKIN IRRITATION MINOR, OR LASTING ONLY FOR A FEW MINUTES. Nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea, elevated temperature following ingestion; skin irritation upon contact with seeds, rootstock, or cell sap." Poison Toxic Principle: "irisin, iridin, or irisine". The Poison Part list, complete as rendered, is Roots, Sap/Juice, Seeds. Separately from that human-scoped block, NC State renders a structured "Problems:" field whose three stacked values are Problem for Cats, Problem for Dogs and Problem for Horses; the cat and dog values are what toxic_to_pets rests on, and the horse value is recorded here for completeness. NC State also lists "Poisonous" as one of five Plant Type traits for this species (Herbaceous Perennial, Native Plant, Poisonous, Water Plant, Wildflower). The structured "Causes Contact Dermatitis" field is answered "No," but note that the same block's Poison Symptoms text reports "skin irritation upon contact with seeds, rootstock, or cell sap" and the page carries a "#contact dermatitis" tag; treat sap and rhizome handling as an irritation risk despite the "No." No admissible source scopes a severity rating or a symptom list to cats or dogs; the pet verdict rests on the Problems field values alone.

records.name_note: Sources split on the lead common name. RHS's dedicated Nuphar advena page leads with 'American spatterdock' beneath the scientific-name heading and lists it first in its own common-name list, an alphabetized run from 'American spatterdock' to 'yellow pond lily' that also includes 'yellow pond lily'. Penn State Extension's Mid-Atlantic Pocket Guide to Water Garden Species instead heads its Nuphar advena entry 'Native Replacement: Spatterdock, Yellow Pond Lily, Yellow Cow Lily', giving three names and no 'American' qualifier -- which also corroborates 'Cow Lily' as an alternate name for this species, in the form 'Yellow Cow Lily'. RHS also records a synonym scientific name for this species, Nuphar lutea subsp. advena. This record lands the RHS dedicated-page lead, title-cased: American Spatterdock.
unknowns: RHS's dedicated Nuphar advena page carries no Cultivation or growing-conditions module at all: a search of the fetched page for Cultivation, How to grow, Position, Hardiness, Soil, Moisture, Sun exposure and pH returns nothing, leaving only Size (Time to Maturity) and a Botanical Details list (Family, Native to GB/Ireland, Genus, Name Status, Plant Range). The Genus row there is genus-level boilerplate about Nuphar and is not read as species culture text. This entry is scoped to RHS alone; it is not the reason the other culture fields are null -- Penn State's species entry supplies what it supplies, and the remaining nulls are disclosed separately.

Penn State Extension's Mid-Atlantic Pocket Guide to Water Garden Species carries a dedicated species-scoped entry for Nuphar advena whose structured items are Max growth height (ft): 1; Flower Color: green-yellow; Bloom Time: March - October; Water Body Type: shallow lakes, ponds, bayous, bogs, streams; Soil Type: sandy, loamy, and clay; Light Requirements: part shade; Hardiness Zones: 4 to 10; and a More Information run. outdoor_sun_exposure is taken from that Light Requirements value. What the guide withholds for this species is a pH or water-quality line (sibling entries in the same guide carry a "Water quality needs:" item and this one does not), any fertilizing guidance, any temperature figure, and any toxicity information, so those fields stay null. The 4-to-10-inch depth figure the research record attributed to this species belongs to the guide's "Deep Water Plants" category definition, not to the Nuphar advena entry.

No toxicity information for Nuphar advena scoped to cats or dogs (or any animal) was found on any of the ten admissible domains, so toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail are left null rather than guessed.

is_houseplant is false. No admissible source states in so many words that this species is not a houseplant, but Penn State's species-scoped entry rates it by outdoor hardiness zone (4 to 10) and places it in shallow lakes, ponds, bayous, bogs and streams, and RHS describes it only as an aquatic pond/water-garden species; neither frames it as an indoor plant.

NC State Extension's Plant Toolbox page found in this search, 'Nuphar luteum (Brandy-Bottle, Spadderdock, Yellow Water Lily),' is for the sibling European species Nuphar luteum, not Nuphar advena, and per scope discipline was not used to support any field on this record even though it carries Light/Soil/pH/Water tags that might otherwise look applicable.

UF/IFAS ask.ifas.ufl.edu content located for Nuphar (e.g. CIR 111/FA163) discusses the genus Nuphar spp. generally in the context of Florida lake vegetation, not a dedicated Nuphar advena species page, so it was not used per the single-species-page requirement.

No admissible-domain content was located for this species on hgic.clemson.edu, plantfinder.mobot.org, www.missouribotanicalgarden.org, edis.ifas.ufl.edu, extension.umd.edu, or fieldreport.caes.uga.edu in this search pass.

No admissible source disputes the name.

Three citations were repaired at landing on provenance grounds. Two quoted the pipe-joined string "Nuphar advena | American spatterdock", which exists only inside the page's <title> metadata; the rendered heading carries the binomial alone and the common name renders separately below it. The third quoted a sentence attributed to Penn State -- "Native spatterdock (Nuphar advena) is a deep-water plant that does well in 4 to 10 or more inches of water." -- that is not on the page: the guide's real text is a bulleted category definition, "Deep Water Plants: these plants do well in 4 to 10 or more inches of water. Waterlilies are common deep-water plants, and many produce showy flowers and impressive leaves. Examples include native spatterdock (Nuphar advena) and fragrant water lily (Nymphaea odorata)." That citation was re-pointed at the guide's own species heading.

Penn State's structured Light Requirements value for this species is "part shade" and nothing else; the same guide writes "Light Requirements: sun, part shade" for other entries, so full sun is affirmatively excluded by the source's own field rather than merely absent. The More Information clause "can survive shaded, deeper waters" is a tolerance clause and was not mapped to full_shade. RHS carries no Position field for this species.

records.cool_rest_note: Clemson HGIC describes the plant dying back to the ground each winter and resprouting in late spring, and specifically warns not to prune back the bare stems after a fall frost -- wait until spring frost danger has passed, since early cutting lets water drip into the stems and freeze, damaging the crown.
records.name_note: Sources split on both the lead common name and the genus. Missouri Botanical Garden's dedicated Plant Finder page carries a single labelled Common Name field reading "scarlet rose mallow"; RHS's dedicated species page renders "American scarlet rose mallow" as its subtitle; UF/IFAS's dedicated page leads its common-name list with the one-word variant, "scarlet rosemallow, Texas star hibiscus, swamp hibiscus"; and Clemson HGIC's dedicated page is titled "Scarlet Swamp Hibiscus". NC State's Common Name(s) list is alphabetized and reads Red Hibiscus, Scarlet Rose Mallow, Texas Hibiscus, in the same order as its page-title parenthetical. "Scarlet Rose Mallow" is used here because, of the three sources whose dedicated page presents a single common name rather than a list (MoBot's labelled Common Name field, RHS's page subtitle, Clemson's article title), two lead with the scarlet-rose-mallow form -- MoBot "scarlet rose mallow" and RHS "American scarlet rose mallow" -- against Clemson's "Scarlet Swamp Hibiscus", and it is the only one of those three forms that also appears in NC State's alphabetized Common Name(s) list. On the scientific name, NC State's Plant Toolbox has moved this species to a renamed genus: its hibiscus-coccineus URL redirects to /plants/muenchhusia-coccinea/, whose page lists "Previously known as: Hibiscus coccineus, Hibiscus semilobatus". RHS's Botanical Details Name Status row for Hibiscus coccineus reads Correct, and MoBot, Clemson and UF/IFAS all still publish under Hibiscus coccineus, so scientific_name_accepted is landed as Hibiscus coccineus with NC State's genus move disclosed here. Distinct from Hibiscus moscheutos (Common Rose Mallow), Hibiscus syriacus (Rose of Sharon) and Hibiscus rosa-sinensis (Chinese Hibiscus) already in this catalog.
